title: Group Selection has the Potential to Increase Yield and Resource Use Efficiency in Cereal Crops
content:
ABSTRACT

The initial stages of crop breeding rely on selecting the best performing individuals, despite these often possessing competitive traits that hinder collective yield. Group selection, where the best-performing groups, rather than individuals, form subsequent generations, is one proposed solution but lacks empirical support. Here we present the results of a group selection experiment targeting protein yield in oat and barley. After eight generations, group-selected oat and barley plants produced higher protein and grain yield than the first generation of plants in the target environment at the beginning of the experiment. Although yield showed an overall positive linear trend across generations, the negative quadratic component indicated a deceleration of this increase, suggesting that further gains may not continue at the same rate. When yield trends were compared with concurrently grown registered cultivars, group-selected plants had higher grain as well as protein yield in barley, whereas no similar trend was detected in oat. Selection for higher group-level yield resulted in a gradual decrease in root production, increased straw production, and sturdier aboveground structures. These trait shifts suggest that increased yield may have been achieved through more efficient allocation to resource-capturing organs. Although the present experimental design does not allow us to fully disentangle the effects of group selection from other processes, such as genetic drift or heterosis, our results indicate that group selection may nevertheless hold potential for improving crop yield and addressing key challenges in sustainable agriculture, warranting further empirical investigation.
